title: Similar / congruent figures: read off corresponding parts
subtitle: Lines, angles, and triangles · 29 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **29 of the official questions in Lines, angles, and triangles are this one** — 4 Easy, 13 Medium, 12 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question says two triangles or polygons are similar, congruent, or related by a dilation, and gives the vertex correspondence, either by listing it or by letter order.
- It asks for an angle in one figure using information about the other figure.
- A scale factor or side lengths are often included as a distraction when the question asks for an angle.
- A variant has a segment drawn parallel to one side inside a triangle and asks for a side length.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Match vertices using the letter order or the stated correspondence, not the picture.
- 2) Corresponding angles are equal, and the scale factor never changes angles.
- If the matched angle isn't given directly, find it with the 180 triangle sum, using any right angle.
- 3) For side lengths when there's a parallel segment: the small and large triangles are similar (AA), so set up small/large = small/large using matching sides and solve.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: It doesn't help with angle questions; the answer comes from matching vertices.
For the side-length variant, you can type the proportion as an equation to solve it, but cross-multiplying by hand is just as fast.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You apply the scale factor to an angle measure, or match vertices by where they sit in the drawing instead of by the stated order.
Wrong choices include the given angle's complement or supplement and the given angle multiplied by the scale factor.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
